newsitem.title: GERMANY: Karstadt - no comment on loss report.
newsitem.headline: Karstadt - no comment on loss report.

text.p: Germany's Karstadt AG on Thursday refused to comment on a magazine report which said its department stores lost money in 1996, leading big shareholders to call for the departure of long-time chief executive Walter Deuss.
A company spokesman said he would "in no way comment" on a report in the Wirtschaftswoche weekly which put the losses at 300 million marks ($177.8 million) and said Deuss's position was in doubt.
He also said he knew nothing of plans to close 50 stores this year reported in Wirtschaftswoche and the Bild tabloid, saying Karstadt had already announced it would close 18 stores.

Wirtschaftswoche said, in a report sourced to unnamed managers, shareholders and labour leaders, that Karstadt would still post a 100 million mark net profit through asset sales and profits at its travel agency and mail order units.

But the company's poor performance was leading to pressure from shareholders -- including Deutsche Bank AG and Commerzbank AG -- for Deuss to step down in favour of 42-year-old logistics director Klaus Eierhoff, the weekly said.
Both banks declined to comment on the reports.

The magazine also said that supervisory board head Guido Sandler wanted to call an urgent board meeting to discuss top personnel issues -- even though Deuss last autumn signed a new five-year contract.
Karstadt shares recovered strongly on the Frankfurt stock exchange after the Wirtschaftswoche report, leading the market higher to close up 21.50 marks at 552.50 marks.
"That can only be because some traders see the obviously possible departure of chief executive Walter Deuss as positive for the company," one trader said.
Despite the bounce, Karstadt shares are still far below their 1995 peak of 678 marks.

The magazine warned that the possible departure of Deuss could lead to changes in accounting practices under a new chief executive which would reveal big hidden losses -- similar to those that rocked auto giant Daimler-Benz AG in 1995 after the departure of chief executive Edzard Reuter.

Karstadt has said it posted sales of 26.9 billion marks in 1996, down 0.3 percent on the previous year. The company said last November it would not be able to match its 1995 net profit of 109 million marks.
Figures calculated under guidelines used by German financial analysts showed that Karstadt lost of 21 marks a share in 1995, down from earnings of seven marks.
Deutsche and Commerzbank own 10 percent each of Karstadt, with a further 30 percent owned by the Hertie foundation representing the Karg family.
